extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and informed general readers interested in sexual selection
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence for judging whether a morphological or behavioural character has arisen through sexual selection (versus protection, mimicry, or other causes), illustrated across insects, fishes, amphibians, and reptiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-limited transmission of variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive variations that are transmitted to and developed in one sex alone can produce sexual differences (sexual dimorphism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that when variations are transmitted only to females or males, characters may become confined to one sex. Example: females imitating protected species while males retain normal congener aspect. Where males lack a variant because those males were eliminated (e.g., less attractive to females), only sex-limited transmission explains the pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female preference (mate choice) driving male ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual selection implies that the more attractive individuals are preferred by the opposite sex, typically females preferring more ornamented males, leading to male ornament evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly as the default explanation where males display colors, appendages, or displays during courtship (but Darwin notes limited direct evidence). Example: male butterflies and dragon-flies with bright colours shown in display; males displaying before females suggests female choice. He also cites behavioural courtship displays (e.g., fishes expanding fins) as support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male–male competition (combat) as a selection mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures used for fighting (weapons, horns, pugnacious behaviour) indicate acquisition via sexual selection through male–male competition for mates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: horns of Lamellicorn beetles, spines on rays, desperate battles of sticklebacks and salmon. Presence of specialized fighting structures and observed injurious battles support competition-driven selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary breeding-season ornaments indicate sexual function
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that appear or intensify only during the breeding-season (e.g., crests, bright colours, spines) are likely sexual ornaments or signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes many fishes and insects gain crests, spines, bright colours only seasonally (e.g., male salmon jaw changes, Blennies’ crests), supporting a sexual rather than general adaptive function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound-producing organs used in courtship imply sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and seasonal use of organs producing calls or songs—especially when used to attract or excite females—indicate evolution by sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Homoptera and Orthoptera males with stridulating organs used during breeding; when both sexes have call-notes, louder/longer callers may gain mates. Darwin treats such organs as acquired through sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments or appendages that seem useless for ordinary life
rubrics_metrics.description: Structures that provide no evident ordinary survival function (e.g., long filaments without muscles, decorative protuberances) are suspect for sexual selection origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites Xiphophorus caudal filaments lacking muscles, Plecostomus hairs, and Chimaera head hook whose ordinary utility is unknown — these are plausibly sexual ornaments even when precise function is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous larval coloration as aposematism (warning coloration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright colours in caterpillars and larvae, coupled with unpalatability or rejection by predators, serve as a warning signal (aposematism) and are selected because predators learn to avoid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin (via Wallace, Jenner Weir, Butler) argues conspicuous caterpillars that are distasteful are readily rejected by birds, implying bright colours evolved to advertise unpalatability. He cautions that this explains conspicuousness but not necessarily the precise palette diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Camouflage/protective coloration vs ornamentation — test by sex and context
rubrics_metrics.description: When both sexes are obscurely coloured, protection (camouflage) is the probable cause; when sexes differ (male bright, female dull) sexual selection or mimicry may explain male ornamentation; when both are bright, mimicry or aposematism may be involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin recommends comparing sexes and ecology: both sexes dull suggests protective selection; both sexes bright could mean mimicry of protected species or resemblance to flowers; male-only brightness often indicates sexual selection, especially when used in display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry of protected species as alternative to sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Bright coloration resembling a protected (unpalatable) species can be an adaptive imitation (Batesian/Müllerian mimicry) rather than sexual ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: female butterflies imitating protected species; Darwin discusses females sometimes made brilliant to imitate protected species, especially when both sexes or females alone show mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontogenetic timing of trait development
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage at which a trait develops (e.g., last moult, maturity, after emergence) informs its selective cause; traits that appear at sexual maturity or just before breeding suggest sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes stridulating organs, dragonfly colours, and bird plumages often develop late (last moult) or soon before breeding, indicating sexual function. Also, males sometimes acquire traits earlier than females, or young resemble adult females.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission/transfer of male traits to females indicates inheritance patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: When traits originally in males appear in females (rudimentarily or fully) in some species, this indicates inheritance/transmission and complicates attribution purely to sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites horns, sound organs, and colours that occur in rudimentary form or are transferred to females, sometimes insufficiently developed for function — consistent with inheritance from male-derived traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlated behavioural evidence of display or courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed behaviours—displaying colours/appendages, nest-building to attract females, elaborate courtship movements—support sexual selection as the causal force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: male Callionymus dragonet displays dorsal fin, Labrus male shows nest and persuasively induces female, Chinese Macropus fishes expand fins and display colours; such behaviors indicate selection through mate attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in sensory/locomotor organs facilitating mate finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex differences in sensory and locomotor organs (males better able to find females) can be adaptive in mating context and indirectly evidence of sexual selection shaping secondary characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin mentions sexes differing in organs of sense and locomotion so males can quickly discover and reach females — these differences support selection linked to mating success rather than general survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative size differences explained by reproductive demands
rubrics_metrics.description: When females are larger than males, consider fecundity selection and life-history (e.g., need for many ova) rather than male–male competition; small males may be selected for earlier development to be ready when females emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes female predominance in size for many fishes and suggests increased female size facilitates ova production; males being smaller may be selected to develop faster for mating opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of ornament presence with group-wide patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same type of coloration or ornament predominates across a whole group, and variation exists among species in male–female differences with intermediate gradations, sexual selection is a plausible common cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses group-level patterns (e.g., butterflies, beetles) to argue sexual selection when many species show similar male ornaments and gradations of sexual dimorphism within the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection behaviour by predators as evidence for warning signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented predator rejection (head-shaking, beak cleaning) of conspicuous larvae supports the hypothesis that bright colours signal unpalatability and are under selection for recognition by predators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites aviary trials where birds rejected hairy, spiny, and conspicuously-coloured caterpillars, showing disgust signals — this behavioural evidence supports aposematism as adaptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of structures for seizing females implies female choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Male specializations (jaws, adhesive cushions, spines, elongated legs) for holding females during copulation suggest females have the power to accept or reject mates, implying sexual selection by female choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin reasons that these male contrivances indicate some difficulty in mating and hence female concurrence is necessary; thus sexual selection via female choice is plausible when such structures are present.
